title: Monthly monitoring of suspended sediment variability using bottle samplers in the LUSI outfall area of the Porong River
author: Yanti, Soemitro, et al.
materials: The highest accuracy was found in column B, which has a more stable flow. In contrast, larger deviations occurred in columns A and C, especially at a depth of 0.8d This difference was caused by local turbulence, the change in the USDH-48 nozzle direction when controlled by a rope, and the difficulty in maintaining isokinetic conditions due to changes in microflow velocity. Furthermore, differences in the operating principles of the instruments contributed to this issue: the vertical water sampler captures water in a closed mode. Closed mode means that water is captured and sealed at a specific depth, preventing it from mixing with water from other layers. At the same time, the USDH-48 relies on passive inflow, which is more sensitive to orientation and local current conditions.

steps.title: Plan sampling stations
steps.instruction: Identify eight cross‑sections along the Porong River from STA 0 + 154 (154 m downstream of the Ginonjo outfall) to STA 6 + 975, spaced approximately 1 km apart, and record their coordinates.

steps.title: Determine water‑column positions
steps.instruction: At each station, define three lateral columns (left bank A, middle B, right bank C), measure the total river depth (d) with a gauge board, and calculate sampling depths of 0.2 d (near surface), 0.6 d (mid‑water), and 0.8 d (near bottom).

steps.title: Prepare USDH‑48 sampler
steps.instruction: Attach flexible vertical and horizontal control ropes to a USDH‑48 bottle (maximum volume 470 mL, use 375–420 mL), set the bottle horizontally with the nozzle facing upstream, and verify rope lengths allow operation at depths greater than 9 m.

steps.title: Measure current velocity
steps.instruction: Using a Valeport 106 current meter, measure flow velocity at each planned depth (0.2 d, 0.6 d, 0.8 d) before sampling.

steps.title: Calculate immersion time
steps.instruction: Compute the immersion time needed for the bottle to fill to 375–420 mL based on the measured velocity, targeting roughly 10 seconds per depth point under assumed isokinetic conditions.

steps.title: Collect USDH‑48 water sample
steps.instruction: Lower the sampler with the vertical rope to the target depth, adjust the nozzle orientation with the horizontal rope to keep it facing upstream, hold the bottle submerged for the calculated immersion time, then raise it and seal.

steps.title: Replicate USDH‑48 sampling
steps.instruction: Perform the USDH‑48 collection twice at each depth‑column point, recording both volumes.

steps.title: Collect validation sample
steps.instruction: Deploy a 500 mL vertical water sampler with messenger system at the same location and depth, lower it, allow stabilization, drop the messenger to close the valve, retrieve the sampler, and keep the sample for analysis.

steps.title: Label and transport samples
steps.instruction: Transfer each water sample immediately into a clean, labeled plastic bottle indicating station, column, and depth; record the volume (average ≈ 400 mL) and transport to the laboratory.

steps.title: Settle and decant supernatant
steps.instruction: Allow the sample to stand until sediment settles, then carefully decant the clear supernatant, leaving about 50 mL of water above the settled sediment.

steps.title: Filter settled sample
steps.instruction: Filter the remaining water through a pre‑weighed Whatman No 42 filter paper (pore size 2.5 µm) following ASTM D3977‑97 Procedure B.

steps.title: Dry and weigh filter
steps.instruction: Dry the filter with retained sediment, weigh the filter plus dried sediment (Wt), and subtract the initial empty filter weight (Wf).

steps.title: Calculate suspended sediment concentration
steps.instruction: Compute SSC (mg L⁻¹) using the formula SSC = (Wt − Wf) × V, where V is the filtered water volume in milliliters.

steps.title: Average replicates and record
steps.instruction: Average the two USDH‑48 replicate SSC values for each point and record the final concentration.

steps.title: Repeat monthly sampling
steps.instruction: Conduct the entire procedure once each month for 12 months (January–December 2023) at the same hour to capture seasonal variability.

description: The method for sampling suspended sediment concentration (SSC) was conducted in the Porong River, East Java, Indonesia, which has been receiving volcanic mudflow from the LUSI (Lumpur Sidoarjo) Ginonjo outfall since 2006. The SSC sampling procedure began at the cross-section upstream of the Ginonjo outfall and extended approximately 7 km downstream. Samples were taken at eight cross-sections, each approximately 1 km apart. Sampling began at STA 0 + 154, which is 154 m from the Ginonjo outfall (STA 0 + 000), and continued up to STA 6 + 975 (Fig. 1).Fig. 1Research Study Location.(Source: Authors modified from Google Earth).Fig 1 At each station (STA), samples are collected from three water columns along the river: the left bank (A), the middle (B), and the right bank (C). Each water column is divided into three vertical depths: 0.2d (near the surface), 0.6d (middle of the water column), and 0.8d (near the bottom), with d being the total river depth measured using a gauge board (Fig. 2). The depth sampling method in this study is based on the concept of vertical distribution, specifically the Equal-Width Increment (EWI) and Equal-Depth Increment (EDI) methods, which are generally used to sample sediments in open waters [2,16,17]. However, these approaches are not explicitly designed for deep, highly turbid tropical river conditions that are difficult to access. Therefore, these basic principles were operationally adapted into depth-proportional procedures (0.2d, 0.6d, and 0.8d) that can be performed from a boat. This procedure enables the acquisition of consistent vertical data in rivers with depths greater than 9 m, even under limited field conditions, providing a practical alternative for tropical river systems that are not yet covered by conventional standards.
